name: Corneal (blink) reflex
function: Protective bilateral eyelid closure (blink) triggered by mechanical or noxious stimulation of the cornea.

steps.cellBodies: Trigeminal ganglion (pseudounipolar neurons of the ophthalmic division, V1)
courseVia: long ciliary branches of the nasociliary nerve
ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1)
steps.terminatesIn: Principal (chief) sensory nucleus of CN V per S10, OR spinal trigeminal nucleus per S9 (see conflicts)
steps.laterality: ipsilateral (afferent limb from the stimulated cornea)

evidence.quote: Sensory information is transmitted via the ophthalmic nerve to synapse within the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the brainstem

an afferent impulse from either free nerve endings or mechanoreceptors within the corneal epithelium is sent by way of nasociliary nerve and its long ciliary nerve branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) to the principal sensory nucleus

the neurones of the first order responsible for the bilateral late reflex on unilateral stimulation terminate in the ipsilateral spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve without significant crossing over to the same structure on the other side.
Its afferent pathway consists of sensory fibres innervating the cornea, that terminate in the nucleus of the spinal tract of the trigeminal nerve
The ipsilateral, short latency orbicularis oculi reflex (R1 component) synapses in the nucleus of the spinal tract of the trigeminal nerve.

steps.cellBodies: Second-order neurons in the spinal trigeminal nucleus (S9) / principal sensory nucleus (S10)
courseVia: bilateral projection to the facial motor nuclei

decussation.where: second-order trigeminal interneurons project bilaterally to the facial motor nuclei

evidence.quote: Neurons in the spinal trigeminal nucleus project to the facial nucleus, forming synapses with the facial nerve

Axons then project bilaterally to facial motor nucleus, which initiating the efferent motor response via the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII), leading to the contraction of orbicularis oculi muscles and coordinated eye closure (blink)
The early, ipsilateral (R1) component of the blink reflex is relayed by interneurons located in the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei
The late, bilateral (R2) component of the blink reflex is relayed by interneurons in the pontine and medullary blink centres
The medullary blink centre receives trigeminal input via multi-synaptic pathways relaying in the tectum and the reticular formation.
The pontine blink centre receives a projection from the rubrobulbar and spinal tract. This connection is used by the cerebellum in conditioning the blink reflex

courseVia: facial nerve (CN VII), encircling the abducens nucleus, exiting at the stylomastoid foramen
steps.laterality: bilateral (early-stage response is predominantly ipsilateral via A-beta fibers; late-stage response is bilateral)

decussation.where: efferent limb itself does not cross further; bilaterality arises from the bilateral second-order projection above

evidence.quote: The late-stage reflex activates facial nerves bilaterally, producing simultaneous blinking of both eyes
The blink reflex protects the eyeball by closing the eyelids through contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscle.
The dorsal subnucleus innervates the frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles.

lesions.deficit: Ipsilateral early-stage blink deficit on stimulation of the affected side (sensory loss); central lesions instead cause bilateral deficits

evidence.quote: Peripheral lesions produce ipsilateral reflex deficits, whereas central lesions result in bilateral deficits

In stage-specific testing, lesions of the trigeminal nerve typically manifest as ipsilateral deficits in the early stage, whereas lesions of the facial nerve produce ipsilateral deficits in both the early and late stages

lesions.site: Lateral medulla / spinal trigeminal nucleus (Wallenberg syndrome, PICA occlusion)
lesions.deficit: Absent late-stage blink response bilaterally upon corneal stimulation of the affected side, because the spinal trigeminal nucleus relaying the reflex is disrupted
lesions.side: bilateral deficit upon stimulation of the affected (ipsilateral) side

evidence.quote: A common lesion that alters the blink response is Wallenberg syndrome, caused by a lateral medullary infarct

unsourced.text: A commonly taught reconciliation of the above conflict is that the fast, largely ipsilateral early blink component is mediated via an oligosynaptic route through the principal sensory nucleus, while the slower, bilateral late component is mediated via a polysynaptic route through the spinal trigeminal nucleus; this reconciling explanation was not itself found stated verbatim in either opened source and is offered here only as an unsourced note, not a citable claim.

S4's full body text (definitions of R1 vs R2 latency values, subject numbers beyond the abstract, and exact lesion localization details) is present only as scanned page images on the PMC HTML page with no OCR; only the abstract text could be opened and quoted verbatim in this session.

A commonly taught reconciliation is that the fast, largely ipsilateral early (R1) blink component is mediated via an oligosynaptic route through the principal sensory nucleus, while the slower, bilateral late (R2) component is mediated via a polysynaptic route through the spinal trigeminal nucleus. Nieuwenhuys instead describes the R1 component as relayed by interneurons in 'the principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei' jointly and the R2 component as relayed by separate 'pontine and medullary blink centres', a somewhat different scheme than the commonly taught reconciliation.
